tasks.title: Implement short-response exercise completion
implementation_targets: exercise completion transaction and read-only saved response UI
Unicode validation and retry conflict handling
tasks.notes: Counting is the whole of this task. PostgreSQL's char_length counts code points and JavaScript's string.length counts UTF-16 units, so a 2,000-emoji response is 2,000 characters to the database and 4,000 to a naive form — the browser would refuse what the database would have accepted. lib/exercise.ts counts by code point and normalises to NFC before counting, and app.normalize_response does the same in SQL. Completion goes through app.settle_completion, the same helper T13's heartbeat calls, so whichever half of a class arrives second completes it and the two paths cannot disagree. PGL40 carries EXERCISE_ALREADY_COMPLETED; an identical resubmission is treated as the retry it is rather than refused.

tasks.title: Implement tutor model adapter and budget accounting
implementation_targets: request dedupe and durable usage reservation/settlement
tasks.notes: Three steps, deliberately separate: ask_tutor reserves under the caller's identity in one transaction that takes the locks and records what the call may cost; the provider is called outside any transaction, because a database transaction must never wait on a network round trip; pglearn_job('tutor.finish') settles through the service-role dispatcher M04 already reserved for it. A crash between two and three leaves the reservation held and the request swept to failed by tutor.reap — spec/05's 'never release unknown usage simply because frontend disconnected'. The reservation counts unresolved reservations at their reserved value and settled ones at what they really cost. PGL43/44/45 carry REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS, RATE_LIMITED and TUTOR_BUDGET_EXCEEDED.

tasks.title: Implement reminder eligibility and outbox claims
implementation_targets: daily cap and transactional outbox claims
tasks.notes: The rules are written twice on purpose: lib/reminders.ts so they can be evaluated against a fixed clock at 08:59 and 09:00 on the day an offset changes, and SQL because only the database can decide them inside the transaction that claims the day. Both use a real IANA timezone database rather than an offset, which is what makes the DST case work — on the morning Madrid's clocks go back, two different instants are the same wall-clock time on the same local date, and the daily claim catches the second. A suppressed message releases its day because nothing was sent; a message already claimed keeps it, because an email in flight cannot be recalled. Nothing with an unknown outcome is ever recorded as failed.

tasks.notes: The adapter's whole job is to distinguish a definitive rejection from an uncertain one: a 4xx that is not 429 means the provider will never send it, and a timeout means nobody knows. The outbox treats those completely differently, so collapsing them into 'error' would silently send somebody two reminders or none. The outbox row's uuid is the provider's Idempotency-Key, which is why a retry must never mint a new one — Resend deduplicates for 24 hours and the behavioural cutoff is 23. The webhook is verified against the RAW body before anything is persisted, and the body is parsed only afterwards; this svix version's verify() returns undefined, so relying on its return value silently turned every valid callback into a 401 until the parse was separated from the verification.

tasks.title: Integrate responsive admin/manager/learner UI
implementation_targets: consistent role navigation and PGLearn branding
checks: Manual keyboard/layout check at 390px and desktop using labeled fixture media
tasks.notes:
One shell, built from get_me: a learner sees their own navigation, a manager of one organization sees it named, a manager of several must choose, and an admin sees the admin items. It is a convenience and not a control — every screen re-establishes the caller's rights from the database.

Two things the work exposed. First, a contract gap: `Program` carries only latest_published_version_id and no operation lists a program's versions, so an author who navigates away from a draft cannot find it again. clone_version — declared in the contract, previously unimplemented — now answers 'give me this program's draft', returning an existing one rather than creating a second. It does NOT copy content: spec/04 defers version cloning, and an asset's storage_key is UNIQUE so a copied class could not carry its media.

Second, an authorization assumption that was wrong: list_programs deliberately answers a MANAGER too, because a manager needs to know what they may assign. The admin pages had inferred admin rights from a refusal, so a manager could open /admin/programs. They now establish platform_admin from get_me. The API refused every write regardless, but the screen should never have rendered.

tasks.title: Add new-version cloning UI and checks
tasks.notes:
T23 created an EMPTY draft and recorded the omission: spec/04 deferred version cloning and an asset's storage_key is UNIQUE, so a copied class could not point at its source's media. T27 is the release that pays it — the target 'independent asset identity/requirements' IS the answer to that problem: the clone owns its own asset rows at its own keys, and the bytes are copied.

Two phases, because storage cannot join the transaction: clone_version copies everything the database owns and creates the new assets pending at the keys their objects must land at; the application copies each file server-side and settles it through the clone.finish job. A file that does not copy leaves its asset failed, which blocks publication — a half-copied clone cannot go live, and the author is told which file to upload again.

Found on the way: the clone route returned {version, created} as its data, but the contract's 201 carries a Version with additionalProperties: false. It now returns the version, and the clone's summary is not returned at all — get_version already reports each asset's state on the screen the author lands on.

tasks.title: Implement retention and verify recovery
checks: Perform restore rehearsal in disposable environment
tasks.notes:
The retention handler is one DELETE per rule from spec/05, in an order the foreign keys allow, each counting what it removed and all of them reading one clock. Every rule deletes on the row's OWN timestamp, never on a parent's, so an active learner does not lose old events and a dormant one does not keep them.

The subtle rule is the tutor ledger: chats go at 30 days and the ledger stays 180, which works only because tutor_usage.request_id has no foreign key to tutor_requests. That absence in the schema is what lets month-end accounting survive the deletion of the chats it accounts for, and a test deletes the chat and re-sums the month.

spec/05's 'purge expired auth links' has nothing to find here: this implementation never puts an Auth action link in the outbox. The statement ships anyway, because spec/05 permits the outbox to hold one temporarily and a job that only purges what today's code writes would silently stop covering tomorrow's.

AC-058 is blocked on performing the rehearsal, not on writing it: the development project has no daily backups, creating and deleting a second project needs authorisation, and the only media in the system is synthetic. tests/evaluation/restore-runbook.md is the procedure and names exactly what is missing.

tasks.title: Measure 40-user load and operational limits
implementation_targets: repeatable bounded load scenario and measurements
tasks.notes:
scripts/load-40.mjs: forty real Auth identities with real enrollments, each calling as itself so row-level security is doing its work on every request, with think time between actions and a single-learner baseline recorded alongside so a slow number can be attributed rather than guessed at.

The first version failed its targets and two of the three reasons were the measurement's fault: it gave every learner a DATABASE BACKEND of their own and fired five reads back to back with no pause. The application does not connect that way — it speaks to PostgREST over HTTPS, which multiplexes onto a small pool — so the measurement now does too.

The third reason was a real finding and is recorded as one: on this instance the connection model dominates everything else. Forty direct backends took p95 from ~200ms to 7-14s while the single-learner baseline was unchanged. Anything in the pilot that opens a connection per user will do the same.

Through the real path: every data operation inside 1s at p95 (slowest 465ms), the dashboard at 1208ms against a 3s target, no failed calls, and no lost acknowledged updates. Measured from this machine to the hosted development project over the public internet, which is a harsher network than the deployed application's.
